newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso suffers blow in re-election drive.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso suffers blow in re-election drive.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso suffered a blow in his campaign to run for a second term on Sunday when the biggest party in Congress voted to delay a bill that would allow his re-election.

A one-day convention of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) decided not to vote until Feb. 15 on a proposal that would let Cardoso run in the 1998 presidential elections and become the country's first re-elected president.

The government, which called an extraordinary session of Congress to get re-election through the Chamber of Deputies in January, had hoped to start voting on the reform on Tuesday in a lower house committee.
"We're back to the drawing board," said a government official in Congress who asked not to be named.

The government's timetable was doomed because the Democratic Movement Party, with 102 of a total 513 deputies, appeared set on ensuring victory for its candidates in upcoming internal congressional elections before voting on re-election, analysts said.

"The PMDB might or might not stick to its decision not to vote on re-election until Feb. 15. But it's clear that there won't be any voting on Tuesday," said Dora Kramer, a political columnist with newspaper Jornal do Brasil.

The convention also recommended its congressmen vote against re-election when it comes to a vote but did not make that recommendation binding, leaving the way open for the government to woo crucial party support.

The Cardoso administration has spent months drumming up support in Congress for re-election, paralysing progress on other reforms considered crucial to the long-term success of its inflation-slashing economic programme.

But the government's attempts to secure the three-fifths majorities it needs for approval of re-election have been thwarted by fighting among allies seeking to win the presidencies of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. Those elections take place in the first week of February.

"The PMDB is playing hardball to get as much as it can," said a party official who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "Delaying the vote will only add to the government's concern about its chances of approving re-election."

Polls published in newspapers O Globo and O Estado de Sao Paulo on Sunday showed the government more than 100 votes short of the 308 lower house votes it needs to approve re-election. Government leaders insist they have 330 votes and say many deputies do not reveal how they will vote to newspapers.
